subject: ventures/surety-bond-capacity-calculator
professional: a contract-surety underwriter / bond producer who sets single-job and aggregate programs for small and mid-size contractors from their CPA statements and WIP schedules

evidence.correctness: Every recomputed output matches. Premium: with the $25/$15/$10 per $1,000 graduated schedule from Old Republic Surety's 'How the Cost of a Contract Bond Is Determined' (Insurance Journal, 2021-10-27), a $1,000,000 contract is $13,500 and a $500,000 one $8,500; `premiumFor(1e6)` / `premiumFor(5e5)` with rate3..5=10 give 13,500 and 8,500. Bond-inclusive price, by hand in tier 3: 0.92P - (8,500 + 0.012(P - 500,000)) = 1,650,000 gives P = 1,652,500/0.908 = 1,819,933.92, premium 24,339.21, profit 145,594.71; tool identical. C=1,000,000, m=8%: P = 1,002,500/0.908 = 1,104,074.89; tool identical. Limits at WC 200k (10x/20x): single 2.0M, aggregate 4.0M, backlog 720k+160k = 880k, headroom 3.12M: match. Overcommit risk of the bid-on-everything set by an independent Python enumeration (scratchpad surety/indep.py): 0.02625 = tool 0.02625. 10x single on WC 250k = 2.5M, matching UHY's worked starting point. Arithmetic is right; what is wrong is method (domain), not sums.
evidence.completeness: `node --test '*.test.mjs'` and plain `node --test` (as the README says): 34/34 pass. Checked each README/page feature via analyze() on the example: tiered premium with credit adjustment and minimum (tests), bond-inclusive price (recomputed), single/aggregate limits and headroom, straight-line burn-down and first fitting month (heavy-job case month 2, recomputed: 3M(1-t/6) <= 2M at t >= 2), best set at zero risk [0,2,4] and within 10% tolerance [0,2,3,4] risk 0.02625, all-bids baseline, working capital needed (fire station 256,389 = 2,563,889/10), WC sensitivity table, CSV with quoted names. served-copy.mjs: no placeholder or retired origin. No stubs or TODOs. Page rendering itself not loaded in a browser.
evidence.verification: 34 tests pass and include a strong independent-recursion oracle for bestSet over 60 random portfolios, hand values for the premium tiers and limits. quality_mutate.py: 3 of 5 core mutants caught (overcommit without backlog, headroom without backlog, earliest-fit threshold). 2 survived, both user-visible columns: 'Fits today' ignoring the aggregate check (calc.mjs:203) and 'Working capital it needs' ignoring current backlog (calc.mjs:179). Every example bid fits the aggregate today and the single-job term dominates in the only wcNeeded test, so neither branch is exercised.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (236 lines), calc.test.mjs, page.test.mjs, index.html module script. Pure exported functions, exact enumeration bounded by MAX_BIDS=6, monotone bisection with a growth guard and a null path that is reported. Defects: negative working capital (a real state for a stretched contractor) is clamped to 0 and answered with 'Enter your working capital', the same as a blank field (run: workingCapital '-50000' -> ok:false, that warning); multiples and rates are clamped silently (single <= 100, rates <= 200) with no warning; money() is an unreadable nested-IIFE one-liner. Nothing a reviewer would block on.
evidence.claims: Disclaimer (No warranty, not legal/tax/accounting/financial advice, verify) at index.html:107 and README; 'Not bonding, financial or legal advice; a surety decides your real rates and limits' at the top; a 'Not decided' list (index.html:99-100) names underwriting, collateral, bid bonds, retainage. Multiples are called rules of thumb and rates placeholders (page.test asserts both). Privacy: page.test asserts no fetch/XHR/beacon; DNT/GPC honoured. Randomised oracle claim backed by calc.test.mjs:95-133. Weak spots: the hero says the tool 'picks the set of bids ... that will not overcommit you' while the default recommendation accepts a 10% chance of overcommitting; '20 is a common rule of thumb' for the aggregate presents the top of a 10-20x range as typical and omits that the cited formulations take the lesser of a working-capital and a net-worth multiple.
evidence.fitness: Walked a contractor's job: enter WC, the agent's rate quote, two running jobs, five bids. Within a minute it gives bond-inclusive prices, which bid is over the single limit, and a submit set; that is a usable bid-pricing aid. The capacity answer is the weak part: with the defaults, WC 200k gives a 4.0M aggregate, while Construction News's surety guidance puts a compiled-statement program around $3M and caps aggregate on tangible net worth; there is no net worth input, no adjusted-WC step, and unbonded backlog is excluded from the aggregate. A contractor who enters their surety's actual limits (converted to multiples) gets a correct answer; one relying on the defaults may bid work their surety will not support.
evidence.domain: Against contractor-surety practice as described by UHY ('lesser of 10-20 times working capital ... [and] 10-20 times total net worth') and Construction News / ACP ('Single Job Limit ~ 8-12 x Adjusted Working Capital', 'Aggregate Program Limit ~ 12-20 x Tangible Net Worth'; underwriters haircut stale receivables and remove underbillings on troubled jobs; internal statements ~ $2M program, compiled ~ $3M, reviewed for more): the single-job 10x WC default sits inside the range and the premium is computed the way sureties publish graduated rates. Departures an underwriter checks first: (1) no net worth / equity constraint at all, so the aggregate can exceed what equity supports (WC 250k, NW 150k: practice ~1.5-3.0M, tool 5.0M at defaults); (2) working capital taken as typed, with no adjusted-WC step (underbillings, related-party and stale receivables, prepaid/inventory haircuts) and no overbilling/underbilling input from WIP; (3) CPA statement level (internal/compiled/reviewed/audited) not modelled although it bounds the program; (4) only bonded backlog counts toward the aggregate, while sureties look at total work on hand. All four are disclosed only generically ('real underwriting looks at much more').

defects.what: Aggregate capacity is working capital times a multiple only; there is no net worth / equity input, although the cited underwriting rules take the lesser of a WC multiple and a (tangible) net worth multiple. A contractor with WC 250k and net worth 150k is shown a 5.0M aggregate at defaults where practice gives roughly 1.5-3.0M.

Working capital is used as typed: no adjusted-WC step (underbillings on troubled jobs, stale/related-party receivables, inventory and prepaid haircuts) and no CPA statement level, both of which an underwriter applies before any multiple; the default 20x aggregate is the top of the 10-20x range and above the ~$3M program a compiled statement normally supports at the example's WC.

Seeded mutants survive in two user-visible outputs: 'Fits today' with the aggregate check removed, and 'Working capital it needs' with current backlog removed. No test has a bid under the single limit but over aggregate headroom, and the only wcNeeded test is dominated by the single-job term.
Only bonded backlog counts toward the aggregate and unbonded bids 'use none of your capacity', while sureties size the aggregate program on total work on hand.
The hero says the tool picks bids 'that will not overcommit you', but the default recommendation accepts a 10% chance of overcommitting (example set risk 2.6%).
Negative working capital is clamped to 0 and answered with 'Enter your working capital', the same as a blank field, instead of saying the multiples give no capacity.

verdict: A correct, well-built bid-pricing aid with an underwriting model thinner than its title. Every recomputed number matches an outside source or hand arithmetic: the graduated premium reproduces Old Republic Surety's $13,500 on a $1M contract, the bond-inclusive price for the library bid is 1,819,933.92 by closed form and in the tool, limits and headroom (2.0M/4.0M/3.12M) and the 0.02625 overcommit probability agree with an independent enumeration. Disclaimer, rule-of-thumb wording and a 'Not decided' list are present. A surety underwriter would stop at the capacity model: aggregate is WC times 20 with no net worth bound, no adjusted working capital (underbillings, receivable haircuts), no CPA statement level and only bonded backlog, so the defaults can overstate capacity well above what the cited practice supports. 34 tests pass, with a real oracle for the bid search, but 2 of 5 seeded mutants survive in the 'Fits today' and 'Working capital it needs' columns. Does not meet the bar (verification 2; correctness 3, claims 3, median 3). Finished (completeness 3). Fixes: a net worth input with aggregate = min(WC x m, NW x n), an aggregate note giving the 10-20x range and its dependence on statement level, two tests pinning fitsNow and wcNeeded on the aggregate branch, and a distinct negative-WC message.
